editor_spans.body: Last week I called the Prime Minister's 'offer' to Holyrood a challenge with nothing in it. My reasoning was that local government in Scotland is devolved, so Westminster has nothing to hand to Scottish regions. The full speech partly corrects me. Its one concrete item is 'DWP devolution': a Scottish model of local employment support, shaped by Holyrood. Employment support is one of the few levers in Scotland that Westminster still holds, so this is a real power to give away, not just a lecture. Even so, it goes to Holyrood rather than to the regions directly, and that confirms the shape I described. Westminster gives something to Edinburgh, then dares Edinburgh to pass it on to the regions.

The longer story behind the speech is one it only half tells. Andy Burnham dates the damage to Ravenscraig and the Lancashire pit closures: decisions 'taken hundreds of miles away' by people who would never live with the results. That loss of trust is one of the main reasons Scotland voted for its own Parliament. Holyrood then pulled power towards itself. It kept just 32 large councils, and its proudest achievements, which Burnham lists himself (public water, nationalised rail, free personal care), are all run nationally. A Parliament created because of distant decisions became a new centre. Burnham's warning that Scottish towns could fall behind northern English cities that are 'powering up' is the first time a Prime Minister has used England's patchwork of mayors as a measuring stick against Holyrood.

The speech's own evidence is weaker than its argument. Its central example, the Easterhouse 'names not numbers' approach, is a local project that worked without any transfer of formal powers. It shows a way of delivering services, not a case for redrawing who holds power. Burnham now wants to scale it up into 'the way we support everybody, everywhere'. That is exactly the kind of national rollout of a local success that has repeatedly failed elsewhere. The other hard proof he offers, buying Alexander Dennis buses, came from bus franchising and procurement choices, not from devolution as such.

Two things to watch. First, the National Economic Council meeting with the devolved First Ministers, the first since he took office, will show whether the employment offer comes with money and a timetable. Second, the welfare framing is significant: one in six young people not in work, education or training, and 'I won't have... kids in their 20s just being there on benefits'. That suggests the devolved employment support will come attached to conditions set by the Treasury and the Milburn review. If so, Holyrood would be taking on the political risk of welfare reform without controlling its terms.

Story 509, the Editor's, made 2026-10-24: "The Prime Minister's 'offer' to Holyrood is really a challenge. Local government in Scotland is devolved, so Westminster has no power to hand Scottish regions anything. It can only shame the Scottish Government by calling it one of the most centralised in Europe. Andy Burnham is offering the city-region model that made his name in Manchester, delivered through No10 North and the Scotland Office. In effect it creates a second route by which Westminster can deal directly with Scottish regions. The Derby headquarters and the East Midlands mayor's comments come from the same playbook. Whether Scotland's First Minister accepts will show whether this is about governing or about positioning."; cited by no later Editor's Span
